meta.subtitle: North America's largest waste operator; Q2'26 brought margin expansion and 34.5% free-cash-flow growth, but a 29.4x P/E caps the entry

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate WM a BUY with a $218-$265 target range. The stock trades at $207.26, near the low end of its $194.11-$248.13 52-week range, after a pullback that leaves a wide-moat, recession-resistant operator available below where the sell side anchors fair value (consensus $259.92). Q2'26 supports the entry: revenue rose {+4.0%+} to $6.7B on 5.7% core price, operating EBITDA margin expanded {+90 basis points+} to 30.4%, and free cash flow grew {+34.5%+} to $1.10 billion. Management reaffirmed 2026 adjusted operating EBITDA of $8.15-$8.25 billion and free cash flow of $3.75-$3.85 billion while trimming the revenue outlook about {-0.6%-} on softer volumes. The counter-case is valuation and the cyclicality of the sustainability businesses: 29.4x trailing earnings leaves little room for disappointment, recycled-commodity and energy prices fell year over year, and Collection and Disposal volume declined 1.8%. Our Base case ($238) assumes WM delivers guidance with pricing above cost inflation; the Bear ($173) prices commodity weakness and multiple compression. Expected upside sits just above the +10% BUY threshold with reward/risk below 1.0x, so we favor a measured position rather than a full one.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Waste Management, Inc. (WM) is, in its own words, North America's leading provider of comprehensive environmental solutions, operating throughout the United States and Canada with additional healthcare-related operations in Western Europe. Founded in 1968 and based in Houston, Texas, the company owns or operates what it calls the largest network of landfills and the largest collection fleet in North America, is the largest recycler, and leads in landfill gas-to-energy, including renewable natural gas (RNG). Management runs the business through five reportable segments: Collection and Disposal - East Tier, Collection and Disposal - West Tier, Recycling Processing and Sales, Renewable Energy, and Healthcare Solutions, the last formed from the acquired Stericycle business. The data set reports WM as a single consolidated line, with FY25 revenue of $25.2B, so we do not attach a revenue split to individual segments. Revenue grew {+14.2%+} in FY25, well above the growth rates of FY22 through FY24, lifted by the Stericycle addition; the solid-waste franchise remains the anchor, complemented by recycling, renewable energy and, now, regulated medical-waste and secure-information-destruction services.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: WM is a wide-moat, defensive compounder whose value rests on irreplaceable landfill assets, route density and pricing power rather than volume growth. In Q2'26 that model showed through: {+5.7%+} core price and {+3.6%+} Collection and Disposal yield drove {+4.0%+} revenue growth even as volume slipped, and operating EBITDA margin expanded to 30.4% as SG&A fell to 10.2% of revenue. Free cash flow of $1.10 billion, up {+34.5%+}, funded buybacks and dividends in the quarter. The stock has de-rated toward the bottom of its 52-week range, and at $207.26 it sits well below the consensus $259.92 target. The bull path is straightforward: deliver the reaffirmed 2026 EBITDA and free-cash-flow guidance, keep capturing Stericycle synergies, and let recycling and renewable-energy projects ramp. The bear path is equally real: at 29.4x earnings the multiple can compress, and the sustainability businesses carry commodity-price risk that turned negative year over year. We think the pullback tilts risk/reward modestly positive.

catalysts: 2026 guidance delivery: management reaffirmed adjusted operating EBITDA of $8.15-$8.25 billion and free cash flow of $3.75-$3.85 billion, with adjusted operating EBITDA margin guided to 31.0%-31.2%.
Stericycle synergies: Q2'26 Healthcare Solutions operating EBITDA grew $25 million on SG&A discipline and integration with core collection operations.

Sustainability projects scaling: three new renewable natural gas facilities (about 3.5 million MMBtu of run-rate production) and a Denver recycling plant (about 60,000 tons of capacity) came online in Q2'26.
Pricing power: core price of 5.7% and Collection and Disposal yield of 3.6% in Q2'26 continue to outrun cost inflation.
Capital returns: WM stepped up share repurchases alongside its dividend in Q2'26, after FY24 buybacks fell to $0.3 billion.
risks: Valuation: WM trades at a premium earnings multiple that leaves little margin for disappointment if execution slips.
Commodity exposure: recycled-commodity and renewable-energy prices fell year over year, pressuring the Recycling Processing and Sales and Renewable Energy segments.
Volume softness: Collection and Disposal volume declined 1.8% in Q2'26, and the 2026 revenue outlook was trimmed about 0.6% on lower volume expectations.
Integration risk: the 10-K flags that Stericycle synergies may not be achieved on the anticipated timeline and could carry added integration costs.
Acquisition leverage: the 10-K warns that growth and acquisitions have caused, and may cause, substantial additional indebtedness.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue climbed from $17.9B in FY21 to $25.2B in FY25, a {+14.2%+} FY25 jump that reflects the Stericycle acquisition folded into the new Healthcare Solutions segment. Profitability did not scale with the top line in FY25: operating margin slipped to 17.1% from 18.4% in FY24, and diluted EPS eased to $6.70 from $6.81, even though EBITDA rose to $7.2B from $6.3B and net income held at $2.7B. Gross margin, by contrast, has trended higher over the period, from 38.0% in FY21 to 40.4% in FY25. The Q2'26 results show the margin story turning back up. Revenue rose {+4.0%+} to $6.7B (reported $6,684 million versus $6,430 million), income from operations increased to $1,253 million from $1,151 million, and GAAP operating margin was 18.7%. On the company's non-GAAP basis, operating EBITDA reached $2,030 million and its margin expanded {+90 basis points+} to 30.4%, overcoming a 60-basis-point headwind from prior-year wildfire-cleanup volumes and a 40-basis-point headwind from higher energy surcharges. Diluted EPS was $1.95 as reported ($2.02 adjusted) versus $1.80 a year earlier. Consensus looks for FY26E EPS of $8.13 and FY27E EPS of $9.12.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The reported balance sheet is conservative. Total equity grew to $10.0B in FY25 from $8.3B in FY24, while the data set shows total debt of $711 million and net debt of $510 million, for net debt to EBITDA of about 0.1x on a trailing basis. Cash and short-term investments were $0.2B at FY25. The current ratio was 0.89 at year-end and 0.91 on a trailing basis; a sub-1.0 current ratio is normal for a route-based collections business that converts receivables quickly. One caution: the reported debt figure looks light against the 10-K's own risk factors, which warn that execution of the growth strategy, including the Stericycle acquisition, has caused and may cause substantial additional indebtedness. We therefore treat the reported leverage reading as understated relative to the acquisition-financed balance sheet the filings describe, and weight cash generation more heavily than the reported net-debt line.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is the core of the WM story. Operating cash flow rose every year from $4.3B in FY21 to $6.0B in FY25, and free cash flow reached $2.8B in FY25 (an 11.2% FCF margin) after $3.2B of capital expenditure. The trailing FCF yield is 4.3%. Q2'26 extended the trend: operating cash flow was $1.73 billion versus $1.55 billion a year earlier, and free cash flow grew {+34.5%+} to $1.10 billion from $818 million. Capital returns are steady and rising: dividends paid grew each year to $1.3B in FY25, and Q2'26 free cash flow funded continued buybacks and dividends, quantified under capital allocation. Management's 2026 outlook calls for full-year free cash flow of $3.75-$3.85 billion, which comfortably covers the dividend and leaves room for continued repurchases and sustainability-growth capital.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: WM trades at 29.4x trailing earnings, 3.2x sales and 11.1x EV/EBITDA, with a forward P/E of 25.5x on next-twelve-month estimates and about 22.7x on FY27E EPS of $9.12. Those are premium multiples that reflect the quality of the asset base and the durability of the cash flows rather than any expectation of rapid growth. The pack does not carry peer multiples (a peer data source is still pending), so we do not benchmark WM against named competitors here; the multiples are assessed against the company's own history and cash-flow profile. The dividend yields 1.82%. Against a consensus target of $259.92 (median $263.00, range $220.00-$277.00) and a Buy-tilted sell side (19 Buy, 9 Hold, 0 Sell of 28 analysts), the market is paying up for a bond-like compounder; the debate is less about business quality than about the price paid for it.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: WM delivers the high end of 2026 guidance (adjusted operating EBITDA near $8.25 billion and free cash flow near $3.85 billion) while pricing stays ahead of cost inflation, Stericycle synergies compound, and recycling and renewable-energy projects ramp. Earnings re-rate toward the top of the analyst target range as the market rewards durable mid-single-digit growth and rising free cash flow.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: WM meets its reaffirmed 2026 outlook: revenue of roughly $26.4 billion, adjusted operating EBITDA of $8.15-$8.25 billion and free cash flow of $3.75-$3.85 billion, with core pricing offsetting soft volumes. EPS advances toward the $8.13 FY26E and $9.12 FY27E consensus, and the multiple holds near its current forward level.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Recycled-commodity and renewable-energy prices stay weak, extending the year-over-year declines seen in Q2'26, Collection and Disposal volumes soften further, and the premium multiple compresses from 29.4x as growth disappoints. Free-cash-flow growth slows and the stock de-rates below its 52-week low.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 45%, the Bull at 30% and the Bear at 25%. The probability-weighted fair value lands modestly above today's $207.26, putting expected upside just over the +10% threshold that separates a BUY from a HOLD. The Bear implied price of $173 sits about 16.5% below the current price, a genuine downside driven by commodity weakness and multiple compression, not a token scenario. Because that bear downside is larger in magnitude than the expected upside, reward/risk screens below 1.0x, which is why we stop at BUY rather than a more aggressive call and favor a measured position size. Our $218-$265 target range brackets the $238 Base case; the low end sits above the current price, so the page's upside line reads positive, and the high end stops short of the Street's $277 ceiling.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The data set reports WM as a single consolidated segment, so the figures here describe the whole company rather than a revenue split. Underneath, management runs five reportable segments. The Collection and Disposal solid-waste business (East and West Tiers) is the anchor and the source of pricing power; its operating EBITDA grew $104 million ($79 million adjusted) in Q2'26 on a favorable price-to-cost spread, even as segment volume fell 1.8%. Recycling Processing and Sales handles paper, cardboard, glass, plastic and metal, where recycled-commodity prices fell year over year. Renewable Energy produces electricity and renewable natural gas that also fuels WM's fleet; three new RNG facilities added about 3.5 million MMBtu of run-rate production in the quarter. Healthcare Solutions, formed from the Stericycle acquisition, provides regulated medical-waste, compliance and secure-information-destruction services. Together the recycling and renewable-energy businesses grew operating EBITDA $39 million (up 32.5%) in the quarter, and Healthcare Solutions grew $25 million.

moatFactors.name: Landfill network
moatFactors.body: WM owns or operates what it calls the largest network of landfills in the U.S. and Canada. New landfill permits are scarce because of land availability and public opposition, a barrier the 10-K itself names, so the installed disposal base is effectively irreplaceable and underpins pricing across the collection chain.

moatFactors.name: Route density and scale
moatFactors.body: A collection fleet described as the largest in North America gives WM route density that lowers per-stop cost and lets it price for yield; Q2'26 core price of 5.7% ran well ahead of cost inflation while operating expenses held at 59.2% of revenue.

moatFactors.name: Regulatory barriers
moatFactors.body: Extensive federal, state, provincial and local regulation raises the cost and complexity of operating landfills and waste services, deterring new entrants and favoring incumbents with permits, compliance infrastructure and scale.

moatFactors.name: Vertical integration
moatFactors.body: Landfill gas-to-energy and RNG let WM monetize its own waste streams and fuel its natural-gas fleet, adding a growth layer to the core; the offset is exposure to commodity prices, which fell year over year in Q2'26.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is durable because its foundations do not erode quickly. Landfill capacity is finite and hard to permit, so the value of WM's existing sites tends to rise, not fall, as the MD&A's reference to diminishing landfill capacity implies. Waste is a mature, comparatively stable industry tied to broad economic activity rather than any single end market, which limits obsolescence risk. The main threats are gradual: waste diversion and recycling mandates that reduce landfill volumes over time, and the intentional shedding of lower-margin residential business, which trimmed Q2'26 volume but is slowing (residential losses improved 210 basis points sequentially). Pricing power has so far more than offset volume softness. The newer sustainability and healthcare businesses widen the platform but bring commodity and integration risk that the core solid-waste franchise does not carry. On balance we assign a WIDE moat.

points: Pricing-led core growth: Q2'26 core price of 5.7% and Collection and Disposal yield of 3.6% drove 4.0% revenue growth despite a 1.8% volume decline; the model grows on price, not tonnage.
Healthcare Solutions scale-up: management aims to take the Stericycle-based segment from integration to scalable growth, and Q2'26 operating EBITDA there grew $25 million.
Sustainability projects: recycling and renewable-energy operating EBITDA rose $39 million (up 32.5%) in Q2'26 as automation and new RNG and recycling capacity came online.

Guidance framework: management targets 2026 revenue of about $26.4 billion, adjusted operating EBITDA of $8.15-$8.25 billion and free cash flow of $3.75-$3.85 billion, implying mid-single-digit growth with margin expansion.
Consensus trajectory: the Street models revenue rising to $27.8 billion and EPS to $9.12 by FY27E, from $25.2 billion and $6.70 in FY25.

management.leadership: James C. Fish, Jr. has been chief executive officer since November 2016; he stepped down as president in May 2025 when John J. Morris, Jr. was promoted to president and chief operating officer. The finance seat turned over recently: David L. Reed became executive vice president and chief financial officer in November 2025, succeeding Devina A. Rankin, who had been CFO since 2020 and served as an executive advisor into March 2026. Tara J. Hemmer has led sustainability as senior vice president and chief sustainability officer since 2021, and Rafael E. Carrasco runs enterprise strategy and the WM Healthcare Solutions business. The bench is deep and largely promoted from within, but the CFO transition is fresh, and investors will watch Mr. Reed's first full cycle of guidance and capital-allocation execution.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is shareholder-friendly and consistent. WM funds heavy reinvestment (capital expenditure was $3.2 billion in FY25) then returns the balance of free cash flow through a growing dividend and buybacks. Dividends paid have risen every year to $1.3 billion in FY25, and the stock yields 1.82%. Repurchases resumed in force in 2026: the company returned $1.04 billion to shareholders in Q2'26 alone, comprising $659 million of buybacks and $379 million of dividends. Management also deploys capital into acquisitions, with the Stericycle deal that became Healthcare Solutions the prime recent example, and into sustainability-growth projects in recycling and renewable energy. With guided 2026 free cash flow of $3.75-$3.85 billion against the dividend, the payout is well covered and leaves ample room for buybacks and growth investment.
management.governance: Governance signals from the 2026 proxy are unremarkable in a good way. The board has adopted a written Related Party Transactions Policy, administered by the Nominating and Governance Committee, that captures transactions above $120,000 in which a director, executive officer, family member or 5%-plus holder has a material interest, with standard carve-outs; officers and directors must notify the chief legal officer of any potential related-party transaction. The proxy excerpt in the pack does not include board-composition or director-independence detail or the executive pay tables, so we cannot assess board independence or say-on-pay outcomes here; the compensation discussion states that a substantial majority of executive pay is linked to company performance through annual cash incentives and long-term equity. We flag the recent CFO transition as the main governance-adjacent item to monitor.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy lists three holders of more than 5% of WM common stock as of March 17, 2026 (on a base of 402,913,509 shares): The Vanguard Group with 36,159,856 shares (9.0%), William H. Gates III together with the Gates Foundation Trust with 28,934,344 shares (7.2%), and BlackRock, Inc. with 28,665,838 shares (7.1%). Ownership is thus dominated by index funds and a large charitable holder rather than concentrated insiders. The excerpt does not quantify director or officer holdings, so we cannot size management's personal stake; note also that the proxy's share basis differs from the 399.72 million shares on the cover-page snapshot we use elsewhere, reflecting different as-of dates.

idiosyncratic: Valuation risk: at 29.4x trailing earnings, 25.5x forward and 11.1x EV/EBITDA, WM prices in continued flawless execution. Any stumble on pricing, volume or margin could trigger multiple compression from a premium base, the central driver of our Bear case.

Commodity-price exposure: the Recycling Processing and Sales and Renewable Energy segments earn on volatile prices. In Q2'26 single-stream recycled commodities fetched about $75 per ton against $84 a year earlier, RFS credits $2.33 against $2.53, and natural gas $2.23 against $2.81 per MMBtu, all headwinds management acknowledges.

Volume softness: Collection and Disposal volume fell 1.8% in Q2'26, and the 2026 revenue outlook was cut about 0.6% on lower volume expectations. Part is intentional shedding of low-margin residential work, but persistent volume loss would pressure the network's operating leverage.

Stericycle integration: the 10-K warns that expected synergies from the Healthcare Solutions segment may not be realized on the anticipated timeline, that ERP and billing disruptions can cost customers, and that integration expenses may exceed expectations.

Acquisition-driven leverage: the 10-K notes that growth and acquisitions have caused, and may cause, substantial additional indebtedness, a reason to treat the data set's low reported net debt (0.1x EBITDA) with caution.
risks.systemic: WM's revenue correlates with general economic activity, since consumer spending, business expansion and construction all feed waste volumes, so a recession would soften volumes even though pricing and the essential nature of the service provide a cushion; the industry is comparatively mature and stable. Inflation in labor, fuel and other costs is a standing pressure that WM offsets through pricing and automation, with mixed timing. Regulation is pervasive: environmental rules on emissions, emerging contaminants, recyclables and extended producer responsibility can raise costs or restrict operations, and permits for new landfill capacity can be blocked by land scarcity or public opposition. Interest-rate levels affect both the cost of the acquisition-financed balance sheet and the relative appeal of a bond-like dividend stock. Finally, commodity and energy markets (recyclables, RNG, RFS credits, electricity) transmit macro price swings directly into the sustainability segments' results.

body: Our conclusion is a BUY. The case is quality at a temporary discount: a wide-moat, cash-generative operator whose shares have pulled back to near the bottom of their 52-week range while the business is still expanding margins and free cash flow. Q2'26 delivered 4.0% revenue growth, 90 basis points of operating EBITDA margin expansion and 34.5% free-cash-flow growth, and management reaffirmed its 2026 EBITDA and cash-flow guidance.

The call is deliberately measured, not emphatic. At 29.4x earnings the valuation is full, the recycling and renewable-energy businesses face real commodity headwinds, and volumes are soft, so the Bear case ($173) is a genuine 16.5% downside and reward/risk screens below 1.0x. We would build the position on weakness rather than chase it, and we would trim if the multiple re-rated toward the Street's $277 ceiling without a commensurate step-up in free cash flow. The pivotal metric to watch is whether core pricing keeps outrunning cost inflation while volumes stay soft.
